title: Opinion: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson should focus on self-control, not birth control
html:
Lululemon founder Chip Wilson speaks after announcing a $100 million donation to preserve and protect B.C.'s natural spaces through his Wilson 5 Foundation, in Vancouver, B.C., Thursday, Sept. 15, 2022. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Darryl DyckDARRYL DYCK/The Canadian Press

Lululemon Athletica Inc. founder Chip Wilson is suffering from a clear case of hysteria.

It is a serious condition that affects untold numbers of unimaginative men. Sufferers are flooded with histrionic emotions about the female uterus, including irrational fears about women’s reproductive choices in both industrialized and developing countries. Risk factors include everyday misogyny, casual racism and a compulsion to put one’s foot in one’s mouth.

Mr. Wilson reportedly experienced a relapse while on stage at a women’s leadership conference in Calgary on Monday. He may have an embarrassment of riches, but money cannot cure what ails him.

Unfortunately for women, Mr. Wilson’s setback was severe. He told attendees that women in Canada often refuse to have as many children as men want. (Imagine that. Canadian women are exercising their agency in 2026.)

The Globe and Mail broke the news about his controversial comments on Tuesday, citing two unnamed sources. The Globe is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to share details about the event.

Mr. Wilson, though, apparently didn’t stop there.

He said that some men may need to import brides from Thailand to have multiple children, according to one of the sources. (Here’s a sample matrimonial ad: Socially inept Canadian male seeks a docile woman of colour to bear his brood. What’s in it for her? Objectification, of course.)

What’s more, Mr. Wilson said birth control had been crucial to women’s advancement in the workplace because it gave business leaders like him the comfort to hire young women without fearing they would immediately take maternity leave. (It’s good to know that a side effect of birth control is the easing of men’s distress when they recruit and promote women at work.)

Mr. Wilson offered conference delegates other pearls of wisdom about women and leadership in the clothing business, but you get the point. As kids today would say, his comments were delulu.

Nonetheless, when The Globe contacted the Lululemon founder’s spokesperson for comment about his remarks, there was no sign of introspection: “This is an effort to discount Chip Wilson’s record of mentoring women who have become executives and entrepreneurs in their own right to drive revenue with a clickbait headline.”

With mentors like that, who needs detractors?

Mr. Wilson, who founded Lululemon in Vancouver in 1998, has a long history of making offensive comments.

In 2004, he made fun of how Japanese people pronounce Lululemon, telling National Post Business magazine, “It’s funny to watch them try to say it.”

Then in 2013, he was forced to step down as the company’s chairman after making disparaging remarks about customers’ bodies. Instead of addressing complaints about the retailer’s yoga pants being too sheer, he told Bloomberg that “some women’s bodies just don’t actually work for [the pants].”

Mr. Wilson left the board entirely in 2015. The following year, he made a remark that denigrated Jewish people.

Although he remains one of Lululemon’s largest shareholders, he has not held a formal role with the company for more than 10 years. Customers, though, still closely associate him with the brand, and thus his comments have continued to cause the retailer grief over the years.

In 2024, for instance, he criticized the company’s diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in an interview with Forbes.

Then, in late 2025, he launched a proxy battle and publicly scolded the company’s board members, accusing them of a “total failure” of oversight. The resolution of that conflict earlier this year required Mr. Wilson to agree to a “non-disparagement” provision. Yeesh.

Arguably, Mr. Wilson’s controversial comments this week have the potential to hurt Lululemon’s brand – and right before the holidays, no less – even if he no longer works there. “So I guess I’ll be skipping @lululemon when Xmas shopping for my daughters this year…” was just one comment posted on social media.

That brings us to the Calgary conference’s organizer, Axis Connects, a non-profit that champions women’s leadership in business. Given Mr. Wilson’s well-chronicled history of gaucherie, why did the organization ever invite him to speak?

As for Mr. Wilson, if he is serious about promoting women’s equality, he should stop talking about our uteruses like they are communal property.

Apologizing is a precursor to realigning his chakras. Prostration might also help him focus on self-control and calm his affliction.

Since he originally took inspiration from my people to build his yoga clothing business, I offer some wisdom from the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, the classic manual written by sage Svatmarama.

“When the breath wanders, the mind also is unsteady. But when the breath is calmed, the mind too will be still, and the yogi achieves long life. Therefore, one should learn to control the breath.”
summary: His comments about women’s reproductive choices at a Calgary conference this week could hurt Lululemon’s brand
